newsitem.title: USA: Stores go after under-aged tobacco buyers.
newsitem.headline: Stores go after under-aged tobacco buyers.

text.p: The government's anti-smoking drive reached into hundreds of thousands of shops in every corner of the United States on Friday with new orders for young tobacco buyers: Prove you're 18 or get lost.

Random checks across the country found many stores complying or saying they intended to comply with the regulation requiring clerks to ask for photo identification of anyone who looks to be younger than 27.

State and federal officials have admitted it would be impossible to monitor compliance at more than a fraction of the estimated half million retail outlets that sell cigarettes and other tobacco products.

The regulations that went into effect on Friday do not cover vending machines, where sales will not be limited until a second phase of the crackdown begins later. And a more intensive compliance drive using under-age undercover operatives in a number of states will not get under way until May.

In Kansas City, Missouri, the manager of a Piggly Wiggly grocery store was reprogramming cash registers so that each machine will lock up when a pack of cigarettes is scanned and will not open until the cashier types in a valid birth date.

"All this is doing is causing a lot of problems for people aged 18 to 27," said the manager, who asked not to be identified. "A 22-year-old can buy a case of whisky and we don't have to card him. But if he wants to buy a pack of cigarettes he's got to go fishing through his pockets for his ID."

At the Tom Thumb Supermarket and Conoco gas station in Maplewood, Minnesota, clerk Sam Emery said "I'm carding everybody. I'm not going to pay a fine. I can't afford that, I have a baby to take care of. When in doubt I card."
The regulations provide for warning letters and fines for stores caught not complying. Fines could be as high as $15,000 for repeat offenders.
Two teenagers strolling through Boston's Faneuil Hall marketplace said they had heard of the new law but their friends who smoke have little difficulty getting tobacco.
"You can get it if you want it," said Joe Lombardi, 16.
"It all matters what store you go to," added his friend Anthony Albano, 15.
Jim Watt, manager at a Pic-Pack convenience store in Louisville, Kentucky, wondered if the regulations would really work since he has seen parents buy cigarettes and hand them to their children.

"We're going to have some uptight people. What it's coming to is that we're just going to have to put up signs that say, 'regardless of age, no ID, no tobacco.' That's the safest thing to do," he said.

Yasamen Smani, who sells cigarettes in a shop near Stuyvesant High School in Manhattan, said customers grew angry when she asked them for IDs. "They said, 'Are you crazy?' and they started to use bad language," she said.
"I do it (require IDs) all the time," said Rahim Jasani at his newsstand a block from New York's Grand Central Terminal. "If I refuse them, some curse me in the face. It's New York."

But the new rules were winning support from some smokers. "I think it's great. Anything they can do to discourage somebody from smoking is good," said Robin Wright, a 31-year-old Kentucky hair stylist who said she has been smoking since she was 12.
